claim: Microsporidia are eukaryotic, obligate intracellular parasites that infect a wide range of hosts.
source: Microsporidia are eukaryotic, obligate intracellular parasites that infect a wide range of hosts, leading to health and economic burdens worldwide.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the scientific literature about microsporidia classification and host range.

claim: Anncaliia algerae microsporidia spores are 3–4 μm in size.
source: Anncaliia algerae microsporidia spores (3–4 μm in size) shoot out a 100-nm-wide PT at a speed of 300 μm/s, creating a shear rate of 3000 s-1.
evidence: Direct measurement of spore dimensions reported in the manuscript.

claim: Anncaliia algerae spores shoot out a 100-nm-wide polar tube at a speed of 300 μm/s.
source: Anncaliia algerae microsporidia spores (3–4 μm in size) shoot out a 100-nm-wide PT at a speed of 300 μm/s, creating a shear rate of 3000 s-1.
evidence: Direct measurement of PT dimensions and velocity from experimental observations.

claim: The polar tube ejection process creates a shear rate of 3000 s-1.
source: Anncaliia algerae microsporidia spores (3–4 μm in size) shoot out a 100-nm-wide PT at a speed of 300 μm/s, creating a shear rate of 3000 s-1.
evidence: Calculated from the velocity and tube dimensions.

claim: The infectious cargo contains two nuclei and is shot through the polar tube for a distance of ∼60–140 μm.
source: The infectious cargo, which contains two nuclei, is shot through this narrow tube for a distance of ∼60–140 μm (Jaroenlak et al, 2020) and into the host cell.
evidence: Cited from previous work by Jaroenlak et al., 2020.

claim: Microsporidia are most closely related to fungi.
source: Microsporidia are most closely related to fungi, but diverged from other species very early in the evolution of the fungal kingdom (Capella-Gutiérrez et al., 2012).

claim: Microsporidia diverged from other species very early in the evolution of the fungal kingdom.
source: Microsporidia are most closely related to fungi, but diverged from other species very early in the evolution of the fungal kingdom (Capella-Gutiérrez et al., 2012).

claim: Microsporidia infection in patients with compromised immune systems can be fatal.
source: Microsporidia infection in patients with compromised immune systems can be fatal (Kotler and Orenstein, 1998).

claim: The overall prevalence rate of microsporidia infection in humans is estimated to be 10.2%.
source: The prevalence of microsporidia is high; a systematic review in 2021 showed that the overall prevalence rate of microsporidia infection in humans was estimated to be 10.2%, and the contamination rate of water bodies with human-infecting microsporidia species is about 58.5% (Ruan et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from a systematic review by Ruan et al., 2021.

claim: The contamination rate of water bodies with human-infecting microsporidia species is about 58.5%.
source: The prevalence of microsporidia is high; a systematic review in 2021 showed that the overall prevalence rate of microsporidia infection in humans was estimated to be 10.2%, and the contamination rate of water bodies with human-infecting microsporidia species is about 58.5% (Ruan et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from a systematic review by Ruan et al., 2021.

claim: Current financial losses in Southeast-Asian shrimp farming due to microsporidia are estimated to be on the order of billions of dollars each year.
source: Current financial losses in Southeast-Asian shrimp farming alone are estimated to be on the order of billions of dollars each year (Stentiford et al., 2016).

claim: Microsporidia are not genetically tractable organisms at this time.
source: Microsporidia are not genetically tractable organisms at this time, which severely limits the study of their biology and infection process.
evidence: Statement about current limitations in microsporidia research.

claim: Anncaliia algerae is a microsporidian species that can infect both humans and mosquitoes.
source: This study focuses on Anncaliia algerae (Figure 1A), a microsporidian species that can infect both humans and mosquitoes (Weiss and Takvorian, 2021).

claim: A. algerae spores can survive in ambient environments for months.
source: A. algerae spores can survive in ambient environments for months (Becnel and Andreadis, 2014).

claim: The protective microsporidian spore coat consists of 3 layers: a proteinaceous exospore, an endospore with chitin as the major component, and a plasma membrane.
source: The protective microsporidian spore coat consists of 3 layers: (1) a proteinaceous exospore, (2) an endospore, of which chitin is the major component, and (3) a plasma membrane.
evidence: Description of spore structure based on established knowledge.

claim: The polar tube is likely an extracellular organelle, topologically outside the plasma membrane but inside the spore wall.
source: It is likely that the PT is an extracellular organelle, which is topologically outside the plasma membrane, but inside the spore wall (Cali et al., 2002).

claim: The polar tube is arranged as a right-handed helix.
source: The PT is arranged as a right-handed helix that interacts closely with other spore organelles, including a vacuole at the posterior end (known as 'posterior vacuole'), and a stack of membranes called the polaroplast at the anterior end.

claim: The posterior vacuole has been previously observed to expand during the germination process.
source: The posterior vacuole has been previously observed to expand during the germination process, and is thus thought to play a role during spore germination, potentially providing a driving force for translocating cargo through the PT (Troemel and Becnel, 2015).

claim: The polaroplast is thought to play a role in the initial stages of the germination process by swelling and exerting a force on the spore wall, causing it to rupture.
source: The polaroplast closely associates with the linear segment of the PT, and is thought to play a role in the initial stages of the germination process by swelling and exerting a force on the spore wall, causing it to rupture (Keohane and Weiss, 1998).

claim: Spores are capable of shooting the polar tube at a peak velocity up to 100–300 μm/s.
source: Spores are capable of shooting the PT at a peak velocity up to 100–300 μm/s (Frixione et al., 1992; Jaroenlak et al., 2020, Figure 1E).
evidence: Cited from Frixione et al., 1992 and Jaroenlak et al., 2020.

claim: Once fired, the extruded polar tube is roughly two times longer than when it is coiled in the dormant spore.
source: Once fired, the extruded PT is roughly two times longer than when it is coiled in the dormant spore (Jaroenlak et al., 2020).

claim: The shear rate experienced by the polar tube is on the order of 3000 s-1, which is an order of magnitude larger than the wall shear rate on the human aorta (300–800 s-1).
source: Considering the thin cross-section of the tube (100 nm), the shear rate (defined as shear per unit time) experienced by the PT is on the order of 3000 s-1, which is an order of magnitude larger than the wall shear rate on the human aorta (300–800 s-1) (Gogia and Neelamegham, 2015).
evidence: Comparison with cited values from Gogia and Neelamegham, 2015.

claim: For A. algerae, the cargo includes two identical nuclei and other organelles.
source: While the exact nature of the cargo being transported through the tube into the host is not known, it is thought that the entire contents of the microsporidian cell are likely to be transported. For A. algerae, this includes two identical nuclei and other organelles.
evidence: Observation of cargo contents in A. algerae.

claim: Cargo transport through the polar tube occurs on a timescale similar to polar tube extrusion.
source: Using these nuclei as a marker, translocation of cargo through the PT has recently been visualized by high-speed imaging (Jaroenlak et al., 2020), showing that cargo transport occurs on a timescale similar to PT extrusion.

claim: At low Reynolds number regime, fluid flow will stop within 10^-9 to 10^-4 s once the boundary movement stops and the driving force disappears.
source: At this Reynolds number regime, the fluid flow will stop within 10-9 to 10-4 s once the boundary movement stops (in this case when the PT is completely ejected) and the driving force disappears (Purcell, 1977).

claim: Serial Block-Face Scanning Electron Microscopy was used to obtain 3D reconstructions of spores in different stages of germination.
source: In order to better understand the physical process of PT extrusion, and changes in PT conformation during the extrusion process, we used SBF-SEM to capture 3D snapshots of spores in different stages of PT extrusion.

claim: 46 spores across three different germination states were reconstructed in 3D.
source: Using segmentation analysis to trace the PT and all other identifiable organelles, we reconstructed 3D models of 46 spores across the three different states.
evidence: Report of number of spores analyzed.

claim: Most germinated A. algerae spores are buckled, resulting in a bean-like shape.
source: In addition, most germinated A. algerae spores are buckled, resulting in a bean-like shape (Figure 1D, Video 3).
evidence: Observation from SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 1D and Video 3.

claim: The posterior vacuole of A. algerae spores expands by roughly 0.35 μm³ during germination.
source: In this study we quantified that the posterior vacuole of A. algerae spores expand by roughly 0.35 μm3 based on the 3D SBF-SEM data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Quantification from SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Posterior vacuoles in germinated spores are significantly larger in volume than posterior vacuoles in ungerminated spores.
source: Posterior vacuoles in germinated spores, (mean=0.955 μm3, std=0.355 μm3, n=14) are significantly larger in volume than posterior vacuoles in ungerminated spores (mean=0.604 μm3, std=0.337 μm3, n=18) (independent t-test, p=0.0260).
evidence: Statistical analysis of measurements from Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increasing methylcellulose concentration up to 4% does not change the germination rate.
source: We found that changing the methylcellulose concentration in germination buffer up to 4%, which corresponds to an increase in viscosity of 103, does not change the germination rate (p-value of logistic regression=0.085, see Supplementary file 3)

claim: Increasing methylcellulose concentration up to 4% does not change the maximum length of the polar tube.
source: We found that changing the methylcellulose concentration in germination buffer up to 4%, which corresponds to an increase in viscosity of 103, does not change the germination rate (p-value of logistic regression=0.085, see Supplementary file 3), maximum length of the PT (p=0.743, Kruskal–Wallis test, see Figure 3—figure supplement 6)
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Increasing methylcellulose concentration up to 4% does not change the peak velocity of polar tube ejection.
source: We found that changing the methylcellulose concentration in germination buffer up to 4%, which corresponds to an increase in viscosity of 103, does not change the germination rate (p-value of logistic regression=0.085, see Supplementary file 3), maximum length of the PT (p=0.743, Kruskal–Wallis test, see Figure 3—figure supplement 6), or the peak velocity of PT ejection (p=0.848, Kruskal–Wallis test, see Figure 3C).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The observation that there is no change in velocity of polar tube firing regardless of external viscosity provides qualitative support to the four hypotheses utilizing an eversion mechanism over the jack-in-the-box ejection mechanism.
source: The observation that there is no change in velocity of PT firing regardless of external viscosity provides qualitative support to the four hypotheses utilizing an eversion mechanism over the jack-in-the-box ejection mechanism.

claim: For the three viable hypotheses (Model 2, Model 4, and Model 5), the total energy requirement is roughly 10^-11 J.
source: It is worth noting that for the remaining three viable hypotheses (Model 2, Model 4, and Model 5), the total energy requirement is roughly 10-11 J, the peak pressure difference requirement is roughly 60–300 atm, and the peak power requirement is roughly 10-10 W, all in a very similar range.

claim: For the three viable hypotheses (Model 2, Model 4, and Model 5), the peak pressure difference requirement is roughly 60–300 atm.
source: It is worth noting that for the remaining three viable hypotheses (Model 2, Model 4, and Model 5), the total energy requirement is roughly 10-11 J, the peak pressure difference requirement is roughly 60–300 atm, and the peak power requirement is roughly 10-10 W, all in a very similar range.

claim: For the three viable hypotheses (Model 2, Model 4, and Model 5), the peak power requirement is roughly 10^-10 W.
source: It is worth noting that for the remaining three viable hypotheses (Model 2, Model 4, and Model 5), the total energy requirement is roughly 10-11 J, the peak pressure difference requirement is roughly 60–300 atm, and the peak power requirement is roughly 10-10 W, all in a very similar range.

claim: The pressure difference requirement for polar tube ejection is comparable to that required for DNA packaging in phages (roughly 60 atm).
source: For example, the pressure difference requirement is comparable or greater than that required for DNA packaging in phages (roughly 60 atm Smith et al., 2001).
evidence: Comparison with cited values from Smith et al., 2001.

claim: 88% of germinated A. algerae spores are buckled inwards.
source: Our SBF-SEM data provide an important clue: 88% of germinated A. algerae spores are buckled inwards (Figure 5C, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Quantification from SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 5C and Supplementary file 6.

claim: All spores in which the nuclei have been ejected have buckled walls.
source: Importantly, all spores in which the nuclei have been ejected have buckled walls, while all incompletely germinated spores, which contain nuclei in them, are not buckled (50 out of 50).

claim: All incompletely germinated spores, which contain nuclei in them, are not buckled.
source: Importantly, all spores in which the nuclei have been ejected have buckled walls, while all incompletely germinated spores, which contain nuclei in them, are not buckled (50 out of 50).

claim: Spore wall buckling correlates with successful nuclear translocation.
source: These observations strongly suggest that spore wall buckling correlates with successful nuclear translocation.
evidence: Inference from correlation observed in SBF-SEM data.

claim: The negative pressure for the spore wall to buckle is only reached when the tube is extended near-completely.
source: This hypothesis further allows the timing of this process to be controlled - where the negative pressure for the spore wall to buckle is only reached when the tube is extended near-completely.

claim: The buckling event is enough to push forward the fluid content inside the polar tube by 129–261 μm.
source: Assuming that the PT is a 100-nm-diameter cylinder, this buckling event is enough to push forward the fluid content inside the PT by 129–261 μm.
evidence: Calculated from displaced volume and PT dimensions.

claim: The distance that fluid can be pushed by buckling is sufficient to propel the nucleus through a completely ejected tube, whose length is between 60 and 140 μm.
source: This distance is sufficient to propel the nucleus to travel through a completely ejected tube, whose length is between 60 and 140 μm (Jaroenlak et al., 2020).
evidence: Comparison of calculated distance with measured PT length from Jaroenlak et al., 2020.

claim: The threshold for water cavitation is about -200 atm.
source: The threshold for water cavitation is about –200 atm (Herbert et al., 2006; Scognamiglio et al., 2018) while the threshold for bubble formation is about –100 atm (Harvey, 1975).
evidence: Cited from Herbert et al., 2006 and Scognamiglio et al., 2018.

claim: The threshold for bubble formation is about -100 atm.
source: The threshold for water cavitation is about –200 atm (Herbert et al., 2006; Scognamiglio et al., 2018) while the threshold for bubble formation is about –100 atm (Harvey, 1975).

claim: For Model 4, 44.4% of spores can have bubble formation.
source: For Model 4, 44.4% of spores can have bubble formation, 7.4% of spores can have spore wall buckling, and none of them can have water cavitation.

claim: For Model 4, 7.4% of spores can have spore wall buckling.
source: For Model 4, 44.4% of spores can have bubble formation, 7.4% of spores can have spore wall buckling, and none of them can have water cavitation.

claim: For Model 5, 88.9% of spores can have bubble formation.
source: On the other hand, for Model 5, 88.9% of spores can have bubble formation, 46.3% can have spore wall buckling, and 20.4% can have water cavitation.

claim: For Model 5, 46.3% of spores can have spore wall buckling.
source: On the other hand, for Model 5, 88.9% of spores can have bubble formation, 46.3% can have spore wall buckling, and 20.4% can have water cavitation.

claim: For Model 5, 20.4% of spores can have water cavitation.
source: On the other hand, for Model 5, 88.9% of spores can have bubble formation, 46.3% can have spore wall buckling, and 20.4% can have water cavitation.

claim: Model 5 has a much better prediction in terms of the fraction of spores that can undergo spore wall buckling compared to Model 4.
source: We can see that Model 5 compared to Model 4 has a much better prediction in terms of the fraction of spores that can undergo spore wall buckling.
evidence: Comparison of model predictions with experimental observations.

claim: Ultrafast polar tube ejection may be useful for the parasites in the context of the extracellular matrix in the host.
source: Ultrafast PT ejection may be useful for the parasites in the context of the extracellular matrix in the host.

claim: As the shear rate increases to 1000 sec-1, the shear viscosity of mucin solutions typically shear-thin by at least 2–3 orders of magnitude.
source: As the shear rate increases to 1000 sec-1, comparable to the physiological shear rate generated by microsporidia, the shear viscosity of mucin solutions typically shear-thin by at least 2–3 orders of magnitude (Sardelli et al., 2019).

claim: The osmotic pressure inside A. algerae spores is estimated to be roughly 60 atm based on prior measurement of sugar content.
source: Based on prior measurement of sugar content in A. algerae spores, we can also estimate the osmotic pressure inside the spores to be roughly 60 atm (see Method for calculation details).
evidence: Calculated from literature data on sugar content.

claim: The total energy provided by posterior vacuole expansion is about 5-fold smaller than the total energy requirement for germination.
source: We can see that although the pressure is comparable to the peak pressure difference requirement (60–300 atm) calculated from our theory, the total energy provided is about 5-fold smaller than the total energy requirement (∼10-11J).
evidence: Comparison of calculated energy from osmotic pressure with total energy requirement.

claim: Posterior vacuole expansion can provide a significant portion of energy but may not be enough to sustain the entire germination process in A. algerae.
source: This indicates that although posterior vacuole expansion can indeed provide a significant portion of energy, it may not be enough to sustain the entire germination process in A. algerae.

claim: Model 5 (E-OE-PTPV-ExP) is the most preferred hypothesis.
source: Combining all evidence, our study suggests that Model 5, E-OE-PTPV-ExP ('Eversion, with original PT content open to external environment, and PT connected to posterior vacuole, with expanding posterior vacuole'), is the most preferred hypothesis (Figure 6).
evidence: Conclusion from combined analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Model 5 predicts that the content of the posterior vacuole should be detectable in the surroundings near the ejected tube after the germination process.
source: First, our model predicts that the content of the posterior vacuole should be detectable in the surroundings near the ejected tube after the germination process.

claim: Model 5 predicts that the cargo would not enter the polar tube until at least half of the tube is ejected.
source: According to our model, we should see that (1) the cargo would not enter the PT until at least half of the tube is ejected

claim: Model 5 predicts that the spores only buckle during the later stage of the germination.
source: According to our model, we should see that (1) the cargo would not enter the PT until at least half of the tube is ejected, (2) the spores only buckle during the later stage of the germination

claim: Model 5 predicts that the sudden translocation of nuclei/cargo coincides with or is slightly later than the buckling of the spore.
source: According to our model, we should see that (1) the cargo would not enter the PT until at least half of the tube is ejected, (2) the spores only buckle during the later stage of the germination, and (3) the sudden translocation of nuclei/cargo coincides with or is slightly later than the buckling of the spore.

claim: The polar tube of A. algerae is about 100-μm-long and only 100-nm-wide.
source: The PT of A. algerae is about 100-μm-long and only 100-nm-wide (Jaroenlak et al., 2020).

claim: Nuclear translocation is not initiated until 50% of the polar tube has been ejected.
source: Previous imaging studies also demonstrate that nuclear translocation is not initiated until 50% of the PT has been ejected (Weidner et al., 1994; Weidner et al., 1995; Jaroenlak et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Weidner et al., 1994; Weidner et al., 1995; Jaroenlak et al., 2020.

claim: Ungerminated spores have a mean volume of 8.78 μm³.
source: Ungerminated: mean=8.78 μm3, std=1.41 μm3, n=19; Germinated: mean=5.52 μm3, std=1.03 μm3, n=14; p<0.0001.
evidence: Measurement from SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Germinated spores have a mean volume of 5.52 μm³.
source: Ungerminated: mean=8.78 μm3, std=1.41 μm3, n=19; Germinated: mean=5.52 μm3, std=1.03 μm3, n=14; p<0.0001.
evidence: Measurement from SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The volume difference between ungerminated and germinated spores is statistically significant (p<0.0001).
source: Ungerminated: mean=8.78 μm3, std=1.41 μm3, n=19; Germinated: mean=5.52 μm3, std=1.03 μm3, n=14; p<0.0001.
evidence: Statistical analysis of measurements from Figure 5D.

claim: Model 1 and Model 3 contradict experimentally observed polar tube firing kinematics.
source: Assuming a cytoplasmic viscosity of 0.05 Pa-s and a no-slip boundary condition, we can see that Model 1 (Figure 4A) and Model 3 (Figure 4C) contradict our experimentally observed PT firing kinematics.
evidence: Comparison of model predictions with experimental data.

claim: Model 1 predicts a significant increase in total energy requirement that cannot be explained by the observed kinematics.
source: Model 1 predicts a significant increase in total energy requirement, which cannot be explained by the observed kinematics.

claim: Model 3 predicts a total energy requirement that varies substantially and is inconsistent with the experimentally observed data.
source: On the other hand, Model 3 predicts a total energy requirement that varies substantially and is inconsistent with the experimentally observed data.

claim: The polar tube ejection process is a tube eversion process in which the polar tube turns inside out as it is extruded.
source: Later experimental evidence, such as microscopic observations of PT extrusion (Thomson, 1959; West, 1960) and pulse-labeling of a half-ejected tube (Weidner, 1982), suggests that the PT ejection process is more likely a tube eversion process, in which the PT turns inside out as it is extruded, such that only the tip is moving during germination.
evidence: Cited from Thomson, 1959; West, 1960; and Weidner, 1982.

claim: The experimental imaging, 3D reconstructions and theoretical analyses support the consensus that polar tube ejection is a tube eversion process.
source: Our experimental imaging, 3D reconstructions and theoretical analyses support the common consensus that PT ejection is indeed a tube eversion process.
evidence: Conclusion from combined experimental and theoretical evidence.

claim: The shape pattern of the ejected tube remains static and does not alter between frames of the movie as the ejection progresses.
source: This is consistent with our observation that the shape pattern of the ejected tube (e.g. the helical or zigzag shape) remains static and does not alter between frames of the movie as the ejection progresses.

claim: The ultrathin nature of the polar tube wall (roughly 5–30 nm) can help reduce the stress associated with the bending of the tube.
source: Also, the ultrathin nature of the PT wall (roughly 5–30 nm Takvorian et al., 2020) can help reduce the stress associated with the bending of the tube, avoiding reaching the yield stress of the PT.

claim: An osmotic pressure of 120 atm (15% saline) suppresses the germination of Nosema bombycis.
source: Ohshima showed that an osmotic pressure of 120 atm (15% saline) suppresses the germination of Nosema bombycis (Ohshima, 1927)

claim: An osmotic pressure of 60 atm (50% glucose) suppresses the germination of Pleistophora hyphessobryconis.
source: while Lom & Vavra showed that an osmotic pressure of 60 atm (50% glucose) suppresses the germination of Pleistophora hyphessobryconis (Lom and Vavra, 1963).

claim: The polar tube emergence time can be prolonged from 1 to 2 s to 10–100 s under hyperosmotic conditions.
source: Undeen and Frixione also report that the PT emergence time can be prolonged from 1 to 2 s to 10–100 s under hyperosmotic conditions (Undeen and Frixione, 1990).

claim: According to Model 5, the membrane connection between polar tube and posterior vacuole must be broken for the infectious cargo to enter the polar tube.
source: Finally, according to Model 5, the membrane connection between PT and posterior vacuole must be broken for the infectious cargo to enter the PT.

claim: Membrane fission mediated by shearing can occur on extremely fast timescales.
source: There are no current data that support membrane fission in this process, but membrane fission mediated by shearing can occur on extremely fast timescales (Morlot and Roux, 2013).
